findings.quote: A constellation seen high in the evening sky in one season is near the Sun's direction, and hidden by daylight, about six months later.
findings.problem: This general statement fails for circumpolar constellations, a known exception. Constellations near the celestial pole never set and are seen every night of the year from places far enough from the equator. At 40 degrees N (a latitude the lesson itself uses in Example #5) Ursa Minor and the Big Dipper stay in the evening sky in every season, and Polaris sits about 40 degrees up all year. The lesson itself teaches that the axis points near Polaris during the whole orbit and calls it our North Star, so the sentence contradicts the lesson's own teaching. It is also only true near the ecliptic: a constellation far north or south of the Sun's path is not 'near the Sun's direction' six months later, even when it is out of the evening sky. A student taught that every constellation is hidden six months later would answer a seasonal-versus-circumpolar question wrongly, and seasonal constellations are a curriculum-class requirement (upcat-L163). The Seasonal Constellations teaching was added in this rewrite, so this is new text.
findings.source: Checklist B01; reader-rules.md 'Added after the Sol audit' (test each general statement against a known exception); Encyclopaedia Britannica, 'circumpolar star' (stars near the celestial pole never set for a given latitude); the lesson's own Revolution and Axial Tilt and Precession sections; brief, upcat-L163 (curriculum)

findings.quote: It is about $4$ minutes shorter because Earth also moves along its orbit during the day.
findings.problem: This Rotation paragraph still has four sentences; the limit is one to three short sentences. Rounds 1 and 2 found this and it is still open. Other paragraphs are also over the limit: the Revolution and Axial Tilt paragraph ending 'The flat surface that the orbit lies on is the **orbital plane**.' has five sentences, and 'Some words first. Earth's **axis** is', 'First, it changes how high the Sun climbs.', '**Rotation** is Earth's spin around its own axis. Earth spins toward the east.' and 'For example, Orion is easy to see in the evening' each have four. This is new or edited content, so these Minor findings must be fixed.
